summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on throughput tuning: discussed continuous batching tradeoffs, concurrency targets, queue depth behavior, and next steps for handoff to steady-state validation. topics: Current pilot metrics and pain points
Concurrency targets and safe upper bounds
Queueing behavior and backpressure / fallback policies
Plan and milestones for handoff to steady-state validation
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Alright good morning everyone, thanks for hopping on. we said 45 minutes so i'll kick off. um quick roll call — priya and i from redwood, and samir elena marcus from neutrino?
[00:07] Samir: Yep that is us, good morning.
[00:11] Priya: hey — quick agenda: run through last week's perf numbers, highlight the outliers, talk through batching and concurrency tweaks we tested, and then agree on the configuration we'll hand off for steady-state runs. sound ok?
[00:21] Elena: sounds good. we had a couple of weird spikes Thursday night that triggered auto-scale, so would like to nail down the guardrails.
[00:29] Jordan: ok great. Priya, you want to take us through the results?
[00:33] Priya: yeah i'll share my screen — uh — okay, so baseline from last monday: target QPS 200, average p95 latency around 220ms for the small transformer variant, token cost roughly in line with expectations. however, when bursts happen we saw queue depth climb and tail latency jump to 1.2s. the cpu on the control-plane host wasn't the limiting factor, looks like batch build latency plus kv cache misses — those amplified under cold sequences.
[01:02] Marcus: does kv cache miss mean the model state was not in GPU memory or the prefix cache? we've seen similar thing in our house infra, but we've got fast local NVMe.
[01:10] Priya: good question. it's the KV prefix cache; when long-conversation sessions rotate between pods, the warmed KV isn't carried across unless sticky routing keeps the session on the same worker. our current pilot was using hash routing which had some churn. that added rebuild overhead for batches which increased per-token latency for the requests that hit the cold path.
[01:35] Elena: curious — sticky routing has tradeoffs for utilization, right? if we make it sticky we might reduce batching opportunities?
[01:41] Priya: exactly — sticky reduces the chance that a batch contains many independent short requests, so it can lower batching efficiency. there's a sweet spot: short sticky sessions for conversations with high KV locality and otherwise allow pooling.
[01:55] Samir: what did you test last week? i remember a config with smaller batch windows?
[01:59] Priya: we tried three configs: 1) conservative — small batch window 3ms, concurrency per worker 8, sticky off; 2) balanced — 10ms window, concurrency 12, sticky by session-id for >20 tokens; 3) aggressive — 25ms window, concurrency 20, sticky on. the balanced was best for average throughput vs p95; aggressive hit higher throughput but tail latency and jitter increased under burst.
[02:27] Jordan: and the customer-visible effect?
[02:30] Priya: balanced kept p95 under 300ms for 95% of runs and allowed sustained QPS 240 on the same capacity. aggressive pushed QPS to ~340 but saw p99 spikes at 1.6–2.0s under 30% of bursts.
[02:45] Marcus: those 1.6s p99s are the ones that triggered our auto-scale rules. our infra team prefers predictable latency over raw QPS — we don't want false positives in scaling.
[02:54] Elena: agreed. also costs are creeping if we keep scaling for every spike.
[02:58] Jordan: so the ask here is to define a safe upper-bound concurrency and queuing policy that avoids those false-positive autoscale triggers while still hitting your throughput goals. what are your target SLOs?
[03:10] Samir: target p95 under 400ms, but p99 ideally under 1.2s. cost budget tradeoff is important — we want to avoid 20% overspend.
[03:20] Priya: ok practical suggestion — for pilot: use balanced config as the handoff baseline, set worker concurrency limit to 14 (not full 20), enable partial sticky routing for session types flagged as long-running, and cap max queue depth at 80 per worker with an early-fallthrough policy after 600ms. that means after 600ms waiting in queue for a token, the request gets routed to fallback model or returns a graceful degrade payload.
[03:47] Marcus: fallback policy sounds good but we need to define the degrade payload — don't want to drop context. can fallback return a short answer and set client-side retry?
[03:55] Priya: yes can be configured to return structured degrade object: reason code, approximate ETA, and optionally a cached summary. clients can decide to retry or surface a soft failure.
[04:05] Elena: how invasive is the early-fallthrough for our client SDK? minimal changes?
[04:09] Priya: minimal — the SDK already understands the degrade envelope we shipped in the POC. it will surface the code and you can opt into automatic retry strategy.
[04:16] Jordan: one risk we flagged: network egress harmonics and pod restart churn during cold cache rebuilds. Marcus, you mentioned pod quotas — did you see pod eviction around the spike windows?
[04:26] Marcus: yes a few nodes hit ephemeral disk pressure and kubelet evicted a non-critical pod which caused rebalancing and then some sessions got rerouted. this amplified the cold KV rebuilds.
[04:34] Priya: recommended mitigation: reserve node-level resources for inference workers and reduce host-level eviction thresholds for pilot. also we can surface a node health metric in the dashboard so you can correlate eviction events to p99 spikes.
[04:46] Samir: would that require infra config changes or can we do a temporary overlay for the pilot?
[04:50] Priya: temporary overlay — a taint/toleration pattern to keep inference pods stable on a dedicated pool; we can provide the manifest snippet.
[04:58] Elena: perfect. about the concurrency number — 14 per worker — is that per GPU or per process?
[05:03] Priya: per GPU-process slot. in your current dedicated nodes each GPU runs one worker process, so it's effectively per-GPU.
[05:10] Samir: ok makes sense. one other question: how will fallbacks affect billing? if we route to a smaller model variant as fallback, do we bill transparently?
[05:18] Jordan: yes fallbacks are model-aware; usage will be billed by model executed. Redwood will show the routing distribution in the console so you can see how much cost was due to fallbacks. we'll also include a small estimate in the handoff doc.
[05:29] Marcus: good. for the synthetic runs — do you have a recommended harness or script we should use to reproduce the same traffic shape? last time our generator didn't emulate the long conversational sessions well.
[05:38] Priya: we'll include the traffic generator config — it includes a session length distribution with heavy tail and a burst pattern file that mirrors your production traces. we'll also attach expected request headers so sticky routing works deterministically.
[05:49] Elena: timeline — you mentioned you'll send the tuned config by Friday?
[05:52] Jordan: yes we'll send the config and the one-page tradeoff sheet by Friday 2027-05-21.
[05:57] Samir: and then we run 3 validation runs and share logs, aiming to have a deep walk-through the week of 5/31?
[06:03] Priya: that's the plan. during the deep walk-through we'll dig into p99 traces and pod-level metrics.
[06:09] Jordan: anything else—legal/security asked for a short SOC2 excerpt and an audit log sample, i can push that to Elena and Samir after the call.
[06:16] Elena: please do, we need it for internal procurement checks.
[06:19] Samir: thanks everyone sounds good — i'm happy with the balanced baseline and the conservative concurrency cap.
[06:25] Priya: cool — to recap action items: redwood will send config + tradeoff doc + manifest overlay; neutrino runs validation; then deep dive.
[06:33] Jordan: great thanks all — we'll follow up in email and i'll put the calendar hold for the week of 5/31.
[06:38] Samir: thanks, bye.
[06:39] Elena: thanks, bye.
[06:40] Marcus: bye.
notes: Key config to try: balanced window 10ms, concurrency cap 14, sticky routing for long sessions, queue cap 80, fallthrough after 600ms
Provide manifest overlay to reserve nodes and avoid pod eviction during pilot
Include traffic generator config and expected headers for deterministic sticky routing
